extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent applicants/practitioners advising examiners or preparing responses)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112 (first paragraph), including how to assess undue experimentation, the relevant prior art and skill level, special considerations for chemical/biological/computer cases, and use of affidavits and deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial inquiry — nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial inquiry is into the nature of the invention, i.e., the subject matter to which the claimed invention pertains. The nature of the invention becomes the backdrop to determine the state of the art and the level of skill possessed by one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what the claimed invention actually relates to before evaluating prior art or skill level; use that definition to scope the pertinent art and skill assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the prior art is judged as of the filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the prior art is what one skilled in the art would have known, at the time the application was filed, about the subject matter to which the claimed invention pertains. The state of the art for a given technology is not static in time ... must be evaluated for each application based on its filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use publications dated after the filing date to demonstrate what was known at filing, except as evidence that those skilled in the art would have known the relevant facts on or before the filing date (see exceptions/cases cited, e.g., In re Hogan, In re Wright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define pertinent art by problem to be solved
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, the pertinent art should be defined in terms of the problem to be solved rather than in terms of the technology area, industry, trade, etc. for which the invention is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the relevant skilled artisan and art by the problem context of the claimed invention to assess enablement and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not disclose what is well-known
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not disclose what is well-known to those skilled in the art and preferably omits that which is well-known to those skilled and already available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not require disclosure of routine or well-known information; case citations provided (e.g., In re Buchner, Hybritech, Lindemann).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement standard — must enable a person skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112 requires the specification to be enabling only to a person 'skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the specification teaches how to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation by a person of ordinary skill as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple arts are involved, enable each specialty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where different arts are involved in the invention, the specification is enabling if it enables persons skilled in each art to carry out the aspect of the invention applicable to their specialty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two distinct technologies are relevant, disclosure must allow a person of ordinary skill in each of the two technologies to practice the invention; see In re Naquin and Technicon Instruments v. Alpkem examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of experimentation is one factor; guidance and predictability matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of experimentation needed to be performed by one skilled in the art is only one factor in determining whether 'undue experimentation' is required. 'The test is not merely quantitative, since a considerable amount of experimentation is permissible, if it is merely routine, or if the specification in question provides a reasonable amount of guidance with respect to the direction in which experimentation should proceed.' Time and expense are merely factors and are not controlling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether experimentation is 'routine' given the guidance in the disclosure, predictability of the art, and other Wands factors; time/expense alone do not establish undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must identify missing information when claiming non-enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: When enablement doubt arises because information is missing about one or more essential parts or relationships between parts, the examiner should specifically identify what information is missing and why the missing information is needed to provide enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections should explain concretely what elements/relationships are unspecified and why a skilled artisan could not fill the gaps without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block diagram / functional disclosure may be non-enabling without details
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure depicted by block diagrams with functional labels can be nonenabling if there is no indication whether parts are off-the-shelf or must be specially constructed, and if the specification lacks details on how parts should be interconnected, timed, and controlled to obtain the claimed operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge components represented as blocks when the specification fails to identify elements, relationships, or how to assemble/adapt complex subassemblies; cite In re Gunn, In re Donohue, In re Scarbrough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex component disclosure may require construction details
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate disclosure of a device may require details of how complex components are constructed and perform the desired function; merely naming complex components generically and stating ultimate functions can be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adaptation of known complex elements to the claimed system would require extensive development work, the disclosure may be non-enabling (see In re Scarbrough).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological materials / microorganism deposits and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions involving living biological products (e.g., microorganisms), availability of the biological material (e.g., via a public depository) can be necessary to meet written description and enablement. A deposit must be made 'prior to issue' though not necessarily prior to filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the scope of the claim (e.g., species vs. strains) relative to what was deposited and whether the verbal description enables production of other claimed members; consult MPEP §2402–§2411.03 and §2411.01 for deposit rules and rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of claims must be commensurate with breadth of enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The breadth of enablement must be commensurate in scope with the claims. Limited examples or narrow direction compared to broad claims, especially in unpredictable arts, can render claims non-enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate number of working examples, predictability of the technology, and amount of direction; examples: Enzo Biochem v. Calgene (antisense overbroad), In re Wright (vaccine claims), In re Goodman (plant cells).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical/art-specific consideration: assay difficulty and quantity of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: In the chemical arts, guidance and ease in carrying out an assay to achieve the claimed objectives may be an issue; a very difficult/time-consuming assay needed to identify a claimed compound contributes to the quantity of experimentation analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider assay difficulty/time and whether experiments required are merely routine; quantity of examples is one factor among others (In re Wands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of post-filing publications — general prohibition with limited exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications dated after the filing date generally cannot be used to show what was known at the time of filing. However, later-dated references may be considered if they provide evidence of what one skilled in the art would have known on or before the effective filing date or if individuals later state the invention was impossible at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on post-filing publications to supply missing disclosure; they may be used as evidence of skill level or impossibility under narrow circumstances (see Chiron v. Genentech, Gould v. Quigg, In re Hogan, In re Wright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-related enablement — present factual analysis and assess all relevant arts
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a reasonable basis for questioning adequacy in computer applications, the examiner must present a factual analysis showing that a person skilled in the art would not be able to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation. When computer programming and another technology are involved, the knowledge of persons skilled in both technologies is the appropriate criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on each block element's functions and how the specification teaches implementation; if more than routine experimentation would be required to implement a component, challenge it under 35 U.S.C. 112 first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block elements more comprehensive than a computer — challenge complex assemblages and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: For systems including a computer plus other hardware/software, scrutinize whether block elements are complex assemblages with differing characteristics requiring precise coordination; without timing charts or sufficient interconnection detail, unreasonable work may be required to achieve claimed functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure lacks precise operations for microprocessors or timing between elements, there may be a reasonable basis to challenge enablement (see In re Ghiron, In re Scarbrough, In re Brown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Block elements within a computer — require operative program or detailed flowchart and prior art reference
rubrics_metrics.description: For pure data-processing applications where block elements are within a computer, adequate disclosure often requires (A) reference to and reliance on an identified prior art computer system and (B) an operative computer program for the referenced system; detailed interrelationships with the hardware are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a program listing or a detailed flowchart tied to an identifiable computer system, a block-element disclosure within a computer should be scrutinized like other block-diagram cases (Knowlton, Comstock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit practice — scrutinize affiant skill and factual support
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits used to rebut an enablement challenge must be critically analyzed: assess the skill level/qualifications of the affiant relative to the routineer; affidavits that present conclusions with few supporting facts are weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affiant with higher-than-routineer skill is less probative; examine factual basis (number of programmers, man-hours, level of skill) supporting claims that routineers could implement the invention (see In re Brandstadter, In re Naquin, In re Morehouse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record support required for examiner challenges in computer cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When USPTO personnel question adequacy of computer system or programming disclosures, reasons for finding the specification nonenabling should be supported by the record as a whole and should reasonably challenge applicant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant presents affidavits or prior art references, examiners must show a reasonable basis for dispute; unsupported conclusory affidavits may be insufficient to rebut examiner positions (In re Naquin, In re Morehouse).
